hook: Air Intelligence Requirements Memorandum Number 4, dated 15 February 1949, is a classified U.S. Air Force standardized protocol establishing exactly how military personnel and allied agencies should observe, document, and report sightings of 'unconventional aircraft and unidentified flying objects, including the so-called Flying Discs.' It was distributed to the FBI, CIA, State Department, Navy, and Coast Guard, explaining its presence in this case file.
why_it_matters: This memorandum reveals the formal, bureaucratically institutionalized infrastructure for UAP reporting that existed by early 1949—less than two years after the 1947 wave—with Wright-Patterson AFB designated as the central collection node for all reports. The document's distribution list, which includes the Director of the FBI, Director of Central Intelligence, and Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence at the State Department, confirms that UAP data collection was treated as a multi-agency intelligence priority, not a marginal Air Force curiosity. Notably, the protocol includes requirements for Geiger counter checks and soil sample collection, indicating that physical trace evidence and radiation were considered serious investigative categories from the outset.

key_findings.finding: Wright-Patterson Air Force Base was designated the mandatory central clearinghouse for all UAP sighting reports from both domestic and overseas commands, with the Commanding General of Air Materiel Command holding authority for direct contact with all reporting organizations.

quotes.text: Reports will be forwarded direct to the Commanding General, Air Materiel Command, Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Dayton, Ohio, Attn: MCIAXO-3 by installations receiv- ing information pertaining to the requirements enunciated in Part II.

Commanding General, Air Materiel Command is authorized direct contact with major Air Commands (ZI) and organizations under their control in connection with the develop- ment of information on this subject.

key_findings.finding: The Air Force formally superseded Army-era UAP collection directives with this memo, consolidating investigative authority and establishing new standardized procedures, signaling an institutional transfer of responsibility in the early post-1947 period.

quotes.text: Department of the Army Collection Memorandum Number 7, dated 21 January 1948, and letter, CSGID 425.1, dated 25 March 1948, both subject as above, which have been transferred to Air Force agencies for action, are herewith superseded.

key_findings.finding: The protocol explicitly required investigators to check aircraft surfaces and landing sites with Geiger counters for radioactivity and to collect soil samples from any location where an object contacted the earth, indicating radiation was an anticipated physical signature from early in the investigation program.

quotes.text: If object came sufficiently near other aircraft or known objects check surfaces with Geiger counters for possible radioactivity. Make comparisons with other unaffected aircraft objects, etc.
If object contacted earth, obtain soil samples within and without depression or spot where object landed (and then presumably departed) for purpose of making comparison of soils.

key_findings.finding: The memorandum's distribution list placed UAP reporting within a broad inter-agency intelligence framework, explicitly routing information to the FBI, CIA, State Department, Navy, and Coast Guard—not solely Air Force channels.

key_findings.finding: Observer reliability assessment was a formal, structured requirement: investigators were directed to cross-reference FBI records, police departments, employers, and neighbors to vet witness credibility, and to note observer fatigue, hobbies (e.g., amateur astronomer, pilot), and ability to estimate speed and size.

legacy_program_connections.reasoning: The memo designates Wright-Patterson AFB (Air Materiel Command, MCIAXO-3) as the mandatory destination for all UAP sighting reports from every command, making it the institutional center of early UAP data collection.

This 1949 Air Intelligence Requirements Memorandum establishes the standardized reporting framework and data categories (observer reliability, radar data, physical evidence) that directly prefigure the Project Blue Book investigative methodology formalized in 1952.
The Director of Central Intelligence appears on the formal distribution list, confirming CIA was a designated recipient of UAP sighting reports from the earliest institutionalized period.
The memo notes that investigators should 'Check Canadian activity if close to that border,' indicating awareness of cross-border UAP activity and coordination with neighboring allied territory.
